defects.description: iam.role_permission_guard (packages/kernel/sql/0120_iam_roles_grants.sql lines 423-427) enforces 'a role never mixes administration and GMP permissions' with a check that takes no lock on the role. Two concurrent iam.add_role_permission calls on the same role, one adding a GMP permission and one adding an ADMINISTRATION permission, each see the role without the other's uncommitted row, so both pass. The second call then waits only on the audit chain-head row lock (an AFTER trigger), after the check has already passed. The per-holder loop cannot catch this either: it only compares the holder's OTHER grants (o.id <> g.id). iam.check_static_segregation also never checks for a mixed role, because it compares across grants only. So the mixed role can be granted to anyone afterwards. This breaks INV-11 and DI-18.
defects.failure_scenario: Reproduced against the unmutated migrations with a scratch vitest outside the repo (scratchpad/defect/race.test.ts). Administrator A: begin; kernel.begin_command; iam.add_role_permission('RACE_MIX','STEP.EXECUTE') (not yet committed). Administrator B, in a second session: begin; kernel.begin_command; iam.add_role_permission('RACE_MIX','IAM.UNLOCK'), which blocks on a transactionid ShareLock (the audit chain head). A commits, then B's call returns successfully and B commits. iam.role_permissions_at('RACE_MIX', now) = {IAM.UNLOCK, STEP.EXECUTE}. The role is then requested and approved for a fresh AUDITOR_READONLY person without refusal. iam.evaluate_authority allows both STEP.EXECUTE (GMP) and IAM.UNLOCK (administration) for that person. iam.directory_scan() returns [] because its ADMINISTRATOR_AND_GMP_ROLE finding needs two different grants (b.id <> a.id). So the INV-11 invariant query also misses the state.
defects.suggested_fix: At the start of iam.role_permission_guard, serialise per role with `perform 1 from iam.role where code = new.role_code for update` (or a transaction advisory lock on the role code) before the line-423 check. Make iam.check_static_segregation take the same role lock (for share) and refuse a role that holds both ADMINISTRATION and GMP permissions (defence in depth). Add a directory_scan finding for a role that mixes the two domains and for a single live grant whose role does. After the fix, add a concurrency test like the race() helper in the mutation test file.

defects.description: Both guards read the permission catalogue at an instant fixed BEFORE they wait for the person-row lock: v_now in iam.check_static_segregation (declared before `perform ... for update`, line 297/303), and new.added_at in iam.role_permission_guard (set at line 420, before the lock at line 436). iam.role_has_domain(..., at) counts only permissions with added_at <= that instant. So a conflicting permission that another transaction adds and commits while this one waits on the lock is invisible when the check finally runs.
defects.failure_scenario: Person P holds roles R and S (both READ-only). T1 runs add_role_permission(R, 'IAM.UNLOCK'), which sets added_at = t1. Before T1 requests P's row lock, T2 runs add_role_permission(S, 'STEP.EXECUTE') with added_at = t2 > t1, takes P's lock first, sees R without administration permissions (T1 uncommitted) and commits. T1 then takes P's lock and checks S for GMP at t1 < t2. S's new row is not live at t1, so T1 commits too. P now holds an administration role and a GMP role. The same interleaving applies to check_static_segregation's v_now against a concurrent permission addition. The window is only the few statements between taking the instant and requesting the lock, so this was not reproduced deterministically.
defects.suggested_fix: After the person lock is acquired, evaluate the catalogue at clock_timestamp() taken at that point, or as 'live now or later' (removed_at is null), instead of at the pre-lock instant. Combined with the role lock above, this closes the window.

All 70 survivors of group segregation-and-grants were killed: `run.ts --group segregation-and-grants --only <all 70 ids> --workers 2` reported 70/70 detected, 0 survived, score 100 % (log in scratchpad/kill-run1.log; report in .reports/sql-mutation/kill-segregation-and-grants). How the kills were done:
- Raw writes run as the table owner (superuser) inside kernel.begin_command, always rolled back, so the audit trigger accepts the mutant's write and the kill does not depend on an unrelated error.
- The two person-row lock mutants (check_static_segregation#6, role_permission_guard#29) are killed by real INV-11 races. Approving a GMP grant races against adding an administration permission to a role the grantee holds, in both orders. Instead of a fixed pause, the race() helper waits until the second session is either finished or waiting on a lock (pg_stat_activity). This is deterministic for both the original and the mutant.
- Most LOGICAL mutants in the role_grant_guard field-change chain are killed by changing exactly one field during a legitimate transition (REQUESTED to APPROVED, or APPROVED to REVOKED). So the mutated guard lets the tampered row through.
- Legitimate catalogue changes kill the over-refusing mutants:
  - removing a permission;
  - adding a GMP permission to a GMP role while other people hold administrator and display roles;
  - adding administration permissions to an administration role;
  - adding a WRITE permission to a service account's role;
  - adding IAM.UNLOCK to a break-glass account's role.

Kills that depend only on the error code (a database constraint would also refuse, but with a different code; codes are the stable API per src/identity/errors.ts):
- role_grant_guard#2: the mutant is refused by the FK (23503) instead of EBMR-IAM-031.
- role_grant_guard#14/#17: the self-revoke is refused by CHECK (23514) instead of EBMR-IAM-003.
- role_grant_guard#22: also killed by behaviour (a REQUESTED insert with decided_by_person goes through).
- role_grant_guard#66: the API call gets IAM-038 instead of IAM-037, but the raw APPROVED-to-REJECTED update kills it by behaviour. That update would remove the grant from past access lists (DI-16).

Kills where the mutant fails open:

Defects: see the defects list. The high-severity one was reproduced against the unmutated code. The low-severity one is an analysed interleaving that was not reproduced. I did not add failing tests for them, because the file must pass on the current code.

defects.description: Not a surviving mutant. I found this while writing the tests. continuity.after_restore calls setval on each registered PG_SEQUENCE while it loops through the protected sources. It checks the counters (EBMR-CONT-023/013) and the maxima (EBMR-CONT-024, registered and unregistered) during the same loop, so some checks run after sequences were already moved. setval is not transactional. When a completion is refused, every sequence moved before the refusal stays moved, but the sequence_bump rows and the audit event are rolled back. INV-27 still holds, because sequences only move forward. What breaks is the rule stated on continuity.sequence_bump that every move of a protected source is recorded, and nothing explains the gap in the numbers.
defects.failure_scenario: The external ledger is incomplete for a counter whose key sorts after the kernel/platform/records sequences, or an unregistered ebmr_owner sequence is close to its maximum. The operator calls after_restore and gets EBMR-CONT-023 or EBMR-CONT-024. By then kernel.audit_event.id has already moved +100,000,000, records.incident.incident_no +100,000, platform.outbox.id +10,000,000, and every other registered sequence by its margin, with no sequence_bump row and no audit entry. Each retry moves them again. The test run observed this: testgmp.pn_small_seq was already at 10 before the successful completion, left there by the refused EBMR-CONT-024 attempt. Users see incident numbers jump by 100,000 with no record of why.
defects.suggested_fix: Split after_restore into two passes. First compute and check every planned move: the counter ledger checks, v_after <= max_value for registered sequences, and v_after <= max_value for unregistered ebmr_owner sequences. Call setval and write the sequence_bump / restore_completion rows only after every check has passed. Alternatively, record refused attempts outside the rolled-back transaction. This is for the owner to decide; no control was changed.

All 46 survivors of the protected-numbers group are now killed and none were classified as equivalent. The harness command was: npx tsx tools/sql-mutation/src/run.ts --group protected-numbers --only <all 46 ids> --workers 2 --out .reports/sql-mutation/kill-protected-numbers. The new file calls continuity.reserve_counter_ceiling and continuity.after_restore directly and asserts each exact refusal message. Groups of tests in the file (only ids that survived before this run are listed):
- Counter tests, [INV-27]:

  - An idempotent retry, or a late lower reservation, returns the ceiling in force and records nothing. Kills #22 and #24.

Their approval of a different event leaves their own event approved. Kills approve#12 and is_approved#11.
  - A successful completion with margin 1, a ledger ceiling equal to the database ceiling, a never-used counter with no ledger entry, a registered and an unregistered sequence moved exactly to their maximum, a stray ebmr_owner sequence bumped and recorded, and nextval above the value it was moved to. Kills #25, #42, #35/#37, #52, #59, #57 and #63.
  - A completed event cannot be approved again, while another pending event is still approvable. Kills approve#8/#7.

Arrangements that bypass the product: one superuser tamper, done with session_replication_role = replica as other suites do. Test sequences created and registered in the testgmp schema. The 'ledger' for after_restore marks is taken from the acknowledged counter ceilings, which is the write-ahead guarantee. No SQL, source, other test, targets.ts or equivalent.json was edited. The one defect reported (low) was not revealed by a mutant; I noticed it while writing the tests, and it is a note for the owner.

Result: 28 of the 31 survivors are now killed. I checked this with the harness: `npx tsx tools/sql-mutation/src/run.ts --group authentication-events --only <all 31 ids> --workers 2 --out .reports/sql-mutation/kill-authentication-events`. The group score is 90.3 % (28/31) against a 90 % target. The new test file passes on the real code (13 tests, about 5 s). `npx tsc -p tsconfig.json` and eslint on the file are both clean. I created only packages/kernel/test/mutation/authentication-events.test.ts. The 0160 definitions are the last ones for all five functions; no later migration redefines them.

What kills what (every refusal is checked by its EBMR code):
- consume_auth_event #7/#8: a COMMAND event and a LOGIN event must be refused with 096 and never consumed.
- consume_auth_event #11: a SIGNATURE event consumed for another challenge, or for no challenge, must be refused with 094. The positive control is that its own challenge consumes it.
- consume_auth_event #15: an event 30 s old with a 10 s window must be refused with 092. So must one called with no window, and one 125 s old with a 1 h window (the policy maximum of 120 s caps the window). The positive control is 30 s old with a 60 s window.
- consume_auth_event #22, two cases, both must be refused with 091: (a) the event attributed a command that committed, and a later transaction reuses the same correlation ID to consume it for a signature; (b) one transaction runs begin_command twice with different correlation IDs.
- use_auth_event_for_command #2, a realistic DI-18 scenario: a system administrator works at a SHARED kiosk and also holds a break-glass account with an approved window. A COMMAND badge-tap event from that break-glass account (same person, other account) must be refused with 122 when used for the personal account's command. The positive control is the holder's own tap.
- open_session #28 and #26: a break-glass LOGIN made while the window was open must not open a session once the window has closed (130). The window is closed by moving its end time back with time-travel setup only, which the test file uses solely to arrange state.
- open_session #3 and #6: a LOGIN event with an unregistered fingerprint must be refused with 070, and with its own device blocked after authentication with 071. Mutant #6 turns `->>` into `->>=` inside the error message, so the refusal fails with "operator does not exist" instead of the EBMR code. After the device is re-activated, the same event opens a session.
- open_session #23: a LOGIN event 121 s old must be refused with 092. The positive control is 100 s old.
- open_session #32, #34 (and #26): a person's READONLY_DISPLAY account logs in on a line display, which is a SHARED device. The person's kiosk session must stay ACTIVE (not superseded) and still accept commands. The display session must have personal=false. The documented rule is that a line display's read-only account does not count against its owner.
- open_session #32 (second test): a SERVICE session must have personal=false, a HUMAN one personal=true.
- session_guard #3/#5: the table owner inserts a session row that is already locked, already ended, or both, in a rolled-back superuser transaction. Each must be refused with 080. The same row inserted open and unlocked is accepted.
- session_guard #9–#30 and #32: each of the 12 fixed columns is updated on its own. Every update must be refused with 081; one column per update kills every or-to-and mutant. Lock and unlock are allowed. Ending the session records the server's time, not the one the writer supplied. After the session has ended, changing locked_at, ended_at or end_reason must be refused with 081.

Still surviving (3), neither equivalent nor a defect. These are consume_auth_event#14 (line 587), use_auth_event_for_command#16 (line 620) and open_session#21 (line 675). Each changes the age check `clock_timestamp() - recorded_at > window` to `>=`. The original matches the contract "no older than the window": an event exactly at the limit is accepted. The mutant would refuse only when the elapsed time equals the window to the microsecond at the moment of the check. That state can occur, so the mutants are not equivalent, but no test can set it up deterministically:
- clock_timestamp() is the real server clock, and search_path puts pg_catalog first, so a test cannot pin it.
- The delay between arranging recorded_at and the check varies by several microseconds from run to run.
- Every window is finite: a policy integer passed through make_interval.
- On this server (PostgreSQL 16.13) infinite intervals do not exist, and subtracting infinite timestamps raises "cannot subtract infinite timestamps" in both versions.

The tests do cover both sides near the limit (100 s accepted, 121 s refused; 30 s accepted with 60 s, refused with 10 s). Killing these three would need a clock seam, such as a kernel "now" that a test fixture can pin. That is a design decision for the owner, not a change I may make.

equivalent_upheld.justification: The mutant turns `v_act is null OR jsonb_typeof(v_act) <> 'object' OR coalesce(v_act->>'device_id','')='' OR coalesce(v_act->>'at','')=''` into `(v_act is null AND jsonb_typeof(v_act) <> 'object') OR C OR D`, because AND binds tighter than OR. Whenever the first or the second term is true, v_act is SQL NULL or a non-object jsonb (null, string, number, boolean or array). For every one of those, the text-field operator `->> 'device_id'` returns NULL without raising, so term C, `coalesce(...,'') = ''`, is already true and ESIG-050 is still raised. When both terms are false, the change makes no difference. None of the terms has a side effect or can raise. The result is identical for every value of p_provided.

This is a clock boundary: `v_act_at > clock_timestamp()` becomes `>=`. The two differ only when the stored act time equals, to the microsecond, the value clock_timestamp() returns inside this comparison. clock_timestamp() is the server wall clock read at evaluation. No caller or role can set or freeze it: search_path pins pg_catalog first, so it cannot be shadowed. The act time is fixed before the call. So no input, stored state or call sequence can produce the equal case deterministically. Any attempt is decided by microsecond timing, not by what the test controls. At the boundary the original accepts an act recorded exactly 'now', which is not in the future, and that is the correct reading.

This is a clock boundary: `clock_timestamp() - v_act_at > v_window` becomes `>=`. The two differ only when the elapsed time equals the witness window (300 s by default) exactly to the microsecond, measured against the clock_timestamp() read inside the comparison. As for check_witness#18, that reading cannot be set, frozen or predicted by any input, state or call sequence, so the difference cannot be observed deterministically. At the boundary the original keeps the window inclusive: an act exactly one window old is 'within the witness window', which is correct.

This is a clock boundary: `clock_timestamp() > v_ch.expires_at` becomes `>=`. The two differ only when the clock_timestamp() read inside the comparison equals the stored expires_at to the microsecond. Time travel can move expires_at to any value, but not to the unknown clock reading taken later inside esig.sign. The clock cannot be frozen or shadowed (pg_catalog is first on the pinned search_path). No input, state or call sequence can observe the difference deterministically. The existing test covers both sides away from the instant: an expired challenge is refused (ESIG-033), a fresh one is accepted.

defects.description: esig.check_witness (0230_esig_sign.sql lines 208-213) fails open under SQL three-valued logic. The ESIG-053 condition is `not v_same and not (v_act_dev.room_code is not null and v_act_dev.room_code = v_sig_dev.room_code and v_act_dev.site_code = v_sig_dev.site_code)`. When the act terminal has a room and the witness terminal has none (room_code NULL, the normal case for PERSONAL devices), `room = NULL` is NULL. The inner AND becomes NULL, `not NULL` is NULL, and `true and NULL` is NULL. IF treats NULL as false, so ESIG-053 is never raised and the witness signature is accepted. The stored witness evidence then reads room_code = the act's room with same_device false, which looks like a valid same-room witness. This breaks the WITNESSED rule (DI-35, outline 5.5 L-03): the witness signs on the act's terminal or on a terminal registered to the same room.
defects.failure_scenario: Reproduced on the current code (temporary test, since removed). A performer on a GRADE_A_B terminal registered to ROOM-X1 creates a stub entry (act = that terminal, now). A VERIFIER on a PERSONAL terminal (no room, same site SITE-1) runs signStub(..., { meaning: 'WITNESSED' }). Expected: EBMR-ESIG-053. Actual: the signature is sealed and committed, with esig.signature.witness = {"room_code":"ROOM-X1","same_device":false,"act_device_id":<performer terminal>,"witness_device_id":<personal laptop>,"window_seconds":300}. A person at a desk can therefore 'witness' an aseptic act they never saw.
defects.suggested_fix: Make the check null-safe and fail closed. For example: `if v_act_dev.id is null or v_sig_dev.id is null then raise ... EBMR-ESIG-053 ...; end if; v_same := v_act_dev.id = v_sig_dev.id; if not v_same and not coalesce(v_act_dev.room_code = v_sig_dev.room_code and v_act_dev.site_code = v_sig_dev.site_code, false) then raise ... EBMR-ESIG-053 ...`. Equivalently, write `(...) is not true`. Add tests: a witness on a room-less terminal is refused with ESIG-053, and the existing same-room and same-terminal tests still pass.

defects.description: Same root cause as the null-room defect. If the provider's act.device_id is a well-formed UUID that names no registered device, `select * into v_act_dev` finds nothing and every v_act_dev field is NULL. Then v_same is NULL and the ESIG-053 condition is `NULL and true`, which is NULL. The witness signature is accepted from any terminal in any room. The stored evidence records act_device_id NULL and same_device NULL. The provider contract (0200: act {device_id, at}) lets any module supply act.device_id. The reference stub always records the validated session device, so today this is reachable through a provider bug or imported data, not through the stub's normal path.
defects.failure_scenario: Reproduced on the current code (temporary test, since removed). A performer on a GRADE_A_B terminal in ROOM-X2 creates a stub entry. As setup, its entered_device_id is set to a random UUID (asTimeTraveller). A VERIFIER on a GRADE_A_B terminal in another room (ROOM-Y9) signs WITNESSED. Expected: refused (unknown act terminal). Actual: accepted, with witness = {"act_device_id":null,"same_device":null,"room_code":null,...}.
defects.suggested_fix: Refuse when the act terminal is not a registered device (for example `if v_act_dev.id is null then raise ... EBMR-ESIG-050/053 the act names an unknown terminal`) and make the room comparison null-safe as in the null-room fix. Add a test in which the act names an unregistered terminal and the witness is refused.

defects.description: iam.assert_validated_actor (0100, via iam.actor_is_validated and kernel.actor_context_validated) only checks that the context JSON in ebmr.ctx has a kernel.command_marker row and an iam.command_log row for the current transaction and backend. It never checks the account or session again. Once kernel.begin_command has validated a context, any role (ebmr_app included) can put it back later in the same transaction with set_config('ebmr.ctx', ctx, true), even after that account was DISABLED, its role grants were revoked and its session ENDED. The FOR SHARE lock in kernel.validate_actor_context only holds off other transactions, so the intent in its comment ("a concurrent deactivation waits for this command") is lost inside the same transaction. This breaks DI-14 and DI-16 (a disabled account can no longer act, and removal takes effect at once) and makes the INV-07 audit attribution wrong: the write is attributed to an account that was disabled when it was made.
defects.failure_scenario: Confirmed on a throwaway database built from all migrations, using only the ebmr_app login role (scratch script /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/0f393df3-64ef-5de6-9328-48ce9ce2b1a5/scratchpad/stale-ctx-app-only.ts). In one transaction: begin_command(ctxA) while operator account A is ACTIVE; then begin_command(admin ctx with a reason) and iam.deactivate_account(A, 'leaver'), which sets A to DISABLED, revokes its OPERATOR grant and ends session S_A; then select set_config('ebmr.ctx', ctxA, true). After that, iam.assert_validated_actor() returns A's context, and an insert into esig.stub_signable is accepted and committed. Its audit event names actor account A with recorded_at 07:58:37.329, 10 ms after A's status_changed_at to DISABLED (07:58:37.319), while iam.session_state(S_A) = 'ENDED'. With ebmr_app and ebmr_authn in one transaction, the same stale context also reaches esig.create_challenge for the person's replacement account B. Only the EBMR-ESIG-010 session-owner guard stops that; the new test covers it.
defects.suggested_fix: Allow only the context most recently installed in the transaction. kernel.set_actor_context (and iam.set_internal_actor) should delete this backend's other command_marker rows for the current xact before inserting the new one, so set_config back to an earlier context fails with IAM-002. Existing code that restores an actor goes through kernel.set_actor_context, so it keeps working. Alternatively, or in addition, iam.assert_validated_actor could re-check at use time that the context's account is ACTIVE and its session is not ENDED, EXPIRED or LOCKED. The owner should decide; no control or SQL was changed.

- required_components#11: the UNLOCKED session event is time-travelled onto the first full signing's instant, which gives PRIVATE; 1 µs later it gives ALL.
- check_independence#12: the exact set of iam.segregation_evaluation rows stored for PERFORMED, VERIFIED and CHECKED.
- check_witness#4/#7/#10: a stub whose act has no terminal, and one with no time, must both be refused with ESIG-050.
- check_witness#13: raw esig.sign with p_next_step_started NULL must give ESIG-051. The same event then signs with false.
- create_challenge#4: unknown signer account gives ESIG-010, not IAM-054.
- sign#7: unknown challenge gives ESIG-031, not ESIG-034.
- sign#19: a second login of the same person on the same PERSONAL device gives ESIG-034.
- sign#25/#28: a context zone of Europe/Berlin gives ESIG-035. #28 (`->>=`) only fails when that raise's message runs.
- sign#31: a forged SIGNATURE event from the same person's active break-glass account gives ESIG-036.
- sign#39/#40: an auth event recorded 1 µs before the challenge is refused; one at the challenge instant is accepted.
- sign#44: a customer meaning text is changed between challenge and sign, giving ESIG-037.
- sign#57: the stub row is deleted, giving ESIG-011 whether the expected state is 'OPEN' or null.
- sign#62: the value is changed with no version bump, giving ESIG-012.
- sign#80: an approved delegation that names VERIFIED (iam.delegation_valid says valid) is still refused with ESIG-041 'cannot be signed under a delegation'.
- sign#89: signer_role_code/name and the manifestation role equal the evaluated role.
- sign#92/#101: a single-connection ebmr_app pool shows esig.signing_challenge and esig.unsealed are empty after commit. With the mutants they keep the ids at session level.

Equivalents: check_witness#18/#20 and sign#14 are clock-boundary mutants. These are observable, so they are not equivalent. The correct behaviour is to treat that instant as "now": a version set for now gets effective_from = recorded_at, the table check is `>=`, and policy_version_at uses `<=`. To hit that exact microsecond, plpgsql probes created in pg_temp write clock_timestamp() + offset in the inserting statement. First they learn the trigger's lag from attempts that are always accepted, then they offer offsets drawn from those lags until one lands exactly on the trigger's reading. Each attempt is rolled back in a subtransaction, and there is a 20 s budget. On real code a hit came within 66 to 1,401 attempts (well under 2 s) over 12 runs. Under the mutants the exact instant is always refused, so the test fails every time. Learning attempts are kept apart from trials so that which trials happen to be accepted cannot skew the learned lags; an earlier version without that separation did fail once.

equivalent_upheld.justification:
With the mutant (0220:309, `v_computed := true` becomes false) the hash `esig.content_hash_of(type, id, esig.provide(type, id))` is recomputed on every loop iteration instead of once per call. Results can differ only if that expression returns different values between two iterations of one call.
(1) content_hash_of is immutable over the provider output, and the provider contract in 0200 forbids a provider from changing data. A non-deterministic provider could never be signed: the hash at the challenge would differ from the hash at signing (EBMR-ESIG-012), so there would be no signature for the loop to visit.
(2) The only writes between iterations are the esig.signature_invalidation row (its stamp trigger and audit trigger) and the kernel.audit_business_event entry (a kernel.audit_event row, action BUSINESS or table esig.signature_invalidation). No trigger on those tables touches a signed table, and no registered provider's hashed fields (content, content_version) read them:
- esig_stub reads only esig.stub_signable.
- sample_record counts only audit events with table_name 'platform.stub_record' and action 'UPDATE'.
- The records and continuity providers have no signed tables. content_changed is owner-private (no grant; migration 0220 comment at line 489), so it runs only from esig.on_signed_content_change and never for those types.
(3) A concurrent commit cannot change hashed content between iterations. content_changed holds the aggregate's transaction-scoped advisory lock (esig.aggregate_lock) until commit, and every other change to that aggregate's hashed content goes through the same trigger, which waits on the same lock before its transaction can commit. For sample_record the changed row's row lock is also held. Only a superuser disabling triggers (session_replication_role = replica) could interleave a change; that is outside the trust boundary and is detected separately by esig.verify_signatures and the INV-09 invariant.
The only difference left is the number of provider calls, which is performance and not behaviour. Checked with a per-mutant run of all 7 new tests plus the group's existing tests: none detects it.

The invalidation trigger for that table is registered with content columns [title, body], so esig.on_signed_content_change calls esig.content_changed only when title or body actually change. An UPDATE that changes no content value still writes an UPDATE audit event. That changes the record's content hash, but no signature is superseded. The provider's hashed content and the signed-table registration disagree. This is outside the mutated functions, but it defeats their purpose for this aggregate type.

**Pitfall I hit:** `select id::text ... order by id` sorts by the text alias, so '10' comes before '9'. The helper orders by `c.id`.

**Defects:** both are in migration 0910 (the sample-record provider), not in the mutated functions. I found them while checking whether #10 could be observed through that provider's audit-count content_version.

defects.description: iam.open_session (kernel 0160) does not serialise with iam.set_device_status (0140). open_session reads the device status without a lock (iam.resolve_device) and inserts the session, whose FK takes only FOR KEY SHARE on the device row. set_device_status UPDATEs the row with FOR NO KEY UPDATE, which does not conflict, and then iam.end_device_sessions ends only the sessions it can see. So a session that is still being opened, not yet committed, survives the block. It stays ACTIVE in iam.session_state and iam.keep_session_alive accepts it. Today only the EBMR-IAM-115 check in kernel.validate_actor_context stops commands in it. After an administrator sets the device back to ACTIVE, the old session can run GMP commands again with no new login. This breaks the DI-20 guarantee that blocked devices' sessions end, which devices-sessions.test.ts states as '[DI-20] blocked and decommissioned devices are refused and their sessions end'.
defects.failure_scenario: Seed a person on a PERSONAL device D and take a LOGIN auth event. Transaction A runs select iam.open_session(ev, fp_D) and stays uncommitted. Transaction B, run as the administrator, calls setDeviceStatus(D, 'BLOCKED', 'suspected tampering') and commits. It is not blocked and ends only the older session. A commits. Verified: the new session's state is ACTIVE and keep_session_alive succeeds. After setDeviceStatus(D, 'ACTIVE', 'inspected'), an insert into testgmp.sample in that session SUCCEEDS with no re-authentication. Found with a temporary probe that was then removed; the committed test asserts only that the command is refused, IAM-115 today.
defects.suggested_fix: In iam.open_session, lock the device row FOR SHARE (select ... from iam.device where id = v_ev.device_id for share) before checking its status, and check the status after the lock. FOR SHARE conflicts with the UPDATE in set_device_status and relocate_device. Then either the sweep sees the committed session, or the login sees the BLOCKED status and is refused. A fix in the sweep could work instead: end_device_sessions could lock the device FOR UPDATE and re-scan after other sessions commit. Add a race test that asserts the session is ENDED or the login is refused.

defects.description: The same missing serialisation exists between iam.open_session and the lockout in iam.authn_finish (0160). open_session checks iam.account_locked once, in iam.lock_auth_event at its start, and does not lock the account row until the FK check at the session insert, which takes FOR KEY SHARE. authn_resolve takes the account FOR UPDATE, so if the lockout runs between those two points, iam.end_account_sessions does not see the new session and it survives the lock. Today only EBMR-IAM-105 in kernel.validate_actor_context stops commands in it. After an administrator calls iam.unlock_account, the escaped session runs GMP commands again with no new login. This breaks the DI-19 guard 'lockout ... sessions end'. A leaver or deactivation that races a login leaves an escaped session on a DISABLED account by the same path. That case is harmless today because DISABLED is terminal and IAM-103 refuses.
defects.failure_scenario: Seed a person on PERSONAL device D, register a second workstation D2 and take a LOGIN event on D. Transaction A calls iam.open_session and is paused at the session's device FK: the test widens the window by holding D's registry row FOR UPDATE in a third transaction. The lock threshold (5) of wrong-password logins then run from D2. The last one locks the account and ends the committed session. Release the row, then A completes and commits. Verified: the account is locked while the new session is ACTIVE. After iam.unlock_account('identity confirmed'), an insert in that session SUCCEEDS with no re-authentication. Found with a temporary probe that was then removed; the committed test asserts only that the command is refused, IAM-105 today.
defects.suggested_fix: In iam.open_session, take select ... from iam.account where id = v_ev.account_id for share before the account and lock checks, or move the lock_auth_event checks after it. FOR SHARE conflicts with the FOR UPDATE in authn_resolve and with the status UPDATE in deactivate_account_internal. Then either the lockout or deactivation sweep sees the committed session, or the login sees the lock or disabled status and is refused. Add a race test asserting that the session is ENDED or the login is refused.

notes:
All 4 actor-validation survivors are killed. Confirmed with the harness: npx tsx tools/sql-mutation/src/run.ts --group actor-validation --only #27,#30,#81,#92 gave 4/4 detected, 100 %. I also ran each mutant alone against only the new file to see which test kills it:
- #27 (EBMR-IAM-104 guard removed). Killed by '[DI-16][DI-14] a person recorded as LEFT cannot act...'. A direct owner write sets iam.person.status to LEFT while leaving the account ACTIVE and the session live, which is the state iam.directory_scan reports as LEFT_PERSON_WITH_LIVE_ACCOUNT. Under the mutant the command SUCCEEDS. Through the API alone this state is unreachable: process_leaver disables every account in the same transaction, account_guard refuses to activate an account of a person who is not ACTIVE, and authn_resolve and lock_auth_event refuse LEFT persons. So IAM-104 is defence in depth against a state the database allows but no constraint prevents. It is not equivalent, and I did not report it as a defect.
- #30 (EBMR-IAM-105 guard removed). Killed by two tests. (a) After a normal lockout the refusal is IAM-105; the mutant gives IAM-112 because the sweep ended the session. (b) In a login that races the lockout, the escaped session is refused as locked; under the mutant the command SUCCEEDS.
- #81 (EBMR-IAM-115 guard removed). Killed by the device-block race test: a session opened while the terminal is being blocked escapes the sweep. Under the mutant the command SUCCEEDS on the BLOCKED device.
- #92 (RELATIONAL at line 124). This is a harness artefact. The '>' it mutated belongs to the named-argument arrow in make_interval(secs => ...), which the mutator turned into 'secs =>= ...'. At run time that is the error 'column "secs" does not exist'. The cause is in mutators.ts: the '=' rule skips when the next character is '>', but the '>' rule lacks a before === '=' skip. The mutant still breaks the path where a personal device sends an auth_event_id. That path had no test in the group, so I added '[DI-14][INV-40] a command on a personal device may carry an authentication event...'. It checks that the event is consumed (auth_event_use COMMAND plus the session), that iam.command_log records it, and that reuse is refused (IAM-126), another person's event is refused (IAM-122), and an event older than authn.event_max_age_seconds is refused (IAM-125) and not consumed.
The race tests use explicit transactions. They never assert that the session survives. They assert only that no command runs in it: the refusal is IAM-112 if the session was swept, IAM-105 or IAM-115 otherwise, or the login itself is refused. They release after at most 3 s if a future fix makes the sweep wait, so they stay valid once the two reported defects are fixed. The file passes on the real code. I ran it 5 times in a row with no flakiness, and together with the group's four identity test files (59 tests passed). tsc -p tsconfig.json exits 0 and includes the file; eslint on the file is clean. The only file I changed is the test file. The scratch script used to map kills to tests is in the scratchpad (which-test-kills.mts).
